In light of the promising results of immune checkpoint blockade (ICPB) in malignant pleural mesothelioma (MPM), we investigated the effect of different chemotherapeutic agents on the expression of immune checkpoints (ICPs) in order to rationally design a good treatment schedule for their combination with ICP blocking antibodies. Cisplatin, oxaliplatin and pemetrexed are interesting chemotherapeutic agents to combine with immunotherapy given their immunomodulatory capacities. We looked into cisplatin and pemetrexed because their combination is used as first-line treatment of MPM. Additionally, the effect of the immunogenic chemotherapeutic agent, oxaliplatin, was also studied. Three different MPM cell lines were used for representation of both epithelioid and sarcomatoid subtypes. The desired inhibitory concentrations of the chemotherapeutic agents were determined with the SRB-assay. Allogeneic co-cultures of MPM cells with healthy donor peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) were set up to assess the effect of these chemotherapeutic agents on the expression of ICPs (PD-1, LAG-3, TIM-3) and their ligands (PD-L1, PD-L2, galectin-9). Cisplatin might be a promising treatment to combine with ICP blocking antibodies since our MPM cell lines were most susceptible to this stand-alone treatment. We found that the expression of ICPs and their ligands on both MPM cells and PBMC was mostly downregulated or unaltered when treated with chemotherapeutic agents, though no clear trend could be determined. chemotherapy tumor microenvironment mesothelioma immune checkpoints MPM PD-1 PD-L1 TIM-3 LAG-3 1. Introduction Malignant pleural mesothelioma (MPM) is an aggressive cancer that affects the membranes lining the lungs. It is causally associated with occupational asbestos exposure and characterized by a long latency period (20−40 years between the inhalation of asbestos fibers and MPM presentation) [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]. Over the years, global incidence has increased steadily with the highest annual rates reported in Australia, Great Britain and Belgium [ 2 ]. Due to its long latency period and the high manufacturing/ usage of asbestos in the late nineties, incidence rates are expected to increase in the following decades [ 4 ] and thus MPM will remain a global health problem. The overall survival and prognosis of MPM patients is very poor with an average survival time of 12 months for untreated patients and a 5-year survival rate of less than 5% [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ]. At the moment, the combination of a platinum-compound (cisplatin) and an anti-folate (pemetrexed) is used as first-line treatment for MPM in the clinic. The combination of both compounds led to a significant increase in median overall survival of approximately 3 months and an increase in total response rate of approximately 30% in comparison with cisplatin stand-alone treatment (12.1 months vs 9.3 months and 41.3% vs 16.7%). These responses suggest a synergism between cisplatin and pemetrexed [ 8 ]. Although this chemotherapeutic strategy plays a very important role in the treatment of MPM, its impact on median overall survival is limited [ 9 ]. The medium survival might be improved through combination with different treatment modalities. For example, the combination of immunotherapy (pembrolizumab) with chemotherapy led to a significant improvement of progression-free survival (from 9 months to a median of 13 months) and higher overall response rates in patients with NSCLC [ 10 , 11 ]. Cancer immunotherapy research entered a new phase with the discovery of immune checkpoints (ICPs), immune modulatory molecules, operating via a series of inhibitory pathways, responsible for maintaining immune homeostasis and modulating immune responses, thereby preventing autoimmunity [ 12 ]. Overexpression of ICPs reduces antitumor immune responses and is suspected to result in an immune resistant tumor [ 12 ]. Therefore, abolishing tumor-immune resistance by blocking ICPs became a promising approach in the field of cancer immunotherapy. In this study, we aimed to investigate the effect of chemotherapeutic agents on the ICP expression of immune cells and MPM tumor cells in order to develop a rational treatment schedule for the combination of chemotherapy with ICP blockade (ICPB). When looking into combination strategies, it is of utmost importance to rationally design a good treatment schedule. Pemetrexed and cisplatin are widely used in the treatment of different types of cancer. Due to the suspected synergistic effect of cisplatin in combination with pemetrexed [ 8 , 13 , 14 ] and the fact that it is used as first-line treatment of MPM patients, we investigated this combination strategy in our study. In addition, oxaliplatin was also included due to its ability to induce immunogenic cell death (ICD) [ 15 ]. ICD distinguishes itself from physiological cell death because of the induced cell structure changes (such as the increased expression of tumor-associated antigens or the emission of danger signals that stimulate immune responses), which allow immune cells to detect these cancer cells and initiate an anticancer response [ 16 ]. On top of that, oxaliplatin has recently shown to be less toxic and more tolerable compared to other chemotherapeutics in gastric cancers [ 17 ]. To date, the combination of chemotherapy with immune checkpoint blockade in MPM has not been described, and therefore, it is not yet known when immunotherapy should be introduced in the treatment scheme. By looking at the effect of different chemotherapeutic agents on the immune checkpoint expression profile of MPM tumor cells and immune cells, we hope to gain more knowledge on which treatment schedule might be best suited for the combination of immunotherapy with chemotherapy. For example, if chemotherapy upregulated the expression of ICPs it might be best to give immunotherapy as an adjuvant treatment. However, in case chemotherapy downregulates ICP expression it would be better to give immunotherapy as a neo-adjuvant treatment. First, we determined the effective concentrations of different chemotherapeutics (cisplatin, oxaliplatin and pemetrexed) to treat mesothelioma cell lines. Then, allogeneic co-cultures of MPM cells with healthy donor peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) were set up. The effect of these chemotherapeutic agents on the expression of ICPs (PD-1, LAG-3, TIM-3) and their ligands (PD-L1, PD-L2, galectin-9) in this co-culture system were assessed with flow cytometry. Analysis with FlowJo provided more detailed information on the effects of the different treatments.

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigated the cytotoxic and immunomodulatory effects of chemotherapeutic agents (cisplatin, oxaliplatin, pemetrexed) on malignant pleural mesothelioma (MPM) cell lines, both alone and in allogeneic co-culture with healthy donor peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC). The primary aim was to assess the impact of these agents on the expression of immune checkpoints (PD-1, LAG-3, TIM-3) and their ligands (PD-L1, PD-L2, galectin-9) to inform rational combination strategies with immune checkpoint blockade. While chemosensitivity varied by cell line (e.g., NCI-H2818 more sensitive to cisplatin and oxaliplatin, no response to pemetrexed), the expression of immune checkpoints and their ligands on MPM cells and PBMCs was mostly downregulated or unaltered, with only TIM-3 on PBMC co-cultured with NCI-H2731 showing significant alteration after cisplatin treatment. The findings generally showed no clear trend or significant changes, highlighting interexperimental variability and suggesting complex interactions relevant for designing optimal immunotherapy combination schedules.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Chemotherapy (cisplatin, oxaliplatin, pemetrexed, and combinations thereof for the core study; other agents like decitabine, doxorubicin, paclitaxel, panobinostat, rituximab, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, prednisone were mentioned for contextual comparison from literature).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Desired inhibitory concentrations (IC values: IC20, IC40, IC50, IC60) for cisplatin, oxaliplatin, and pemetrexed were determined via SRB-assay across three MPM cell lines (NCI-H2818, NCI-H2795, NCI-H2731). Specific concentration ranges tested were cisplatin (0-50  5M), oxaliplatin (0-50  5M), and pemetrexed (0-10  5M). For further co-culture experiments, IC20 values were typically used, with 0.05  5M specifically mentioned for pemetrexed. All treatments were applied for 72 hours. Susceptibility to cisplatin and oxaliplatin was cell-line dependent (e.g., NCI-H2818 was significantly more sensitive to both), while pemetrexed showed no cytotoxic response in any cell line. No significant difference in cell survival was observed between cisplatin and cisplatin + pemetrexed treatment groups. PBMC were co-cultured with MPM cells at a 10:1 (Effector:Target) ratio. The study acknowledged significant interexperimental variability and inconsistency in effects on immune checkpoint expression across different studies and agents.

analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: MPM cells and healthy donor peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC), also referenced in normal lymphocytes and leukemia cells.
analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Protein Level (Expression assessed by flow cytometry; percentage of positive cells and intensity/MFI values)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Mostly downregulated or unaltered across various chemotherapeutic treatments (cisplatin, oxaliplatin, pemetrexed) with no clear overall trend. No significant differences were found in the percentage of PD-1 positive cells or its expression intensity (MFI) compared to untreated groups in co-culture experiments. However, contextual references noted both decrease (e.g., panobinostat in Hodgkin lymphoma lymphocytes) and enhancement (e.g., decitabine in leukemia cells) in PD-1 expression by chemotherapy in other cancer types.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Immune modulatory molecule and checkpoint operating via inhibitory pathways to maintain immune homeostasis and modulate immune responses, preventing autoimmunity. Overexpression reduces antitumor immune responses.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Treatment of MPM cell lines (NCI-H2818, NCI-H2795, NCI-H2731) in allogeneic co-cultures with healthy donor PBMCs using various chemotherapeutic agents (cisplatin, oxaliplatin, pemetrexed) for 72 hours. Comparisons to other chemotherapies (panobinostat, decitabine) in different cancer types were also made.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Overexpression reduces antitumor immune responses, potentially leading to immune-resistant tumors. Blocking PD-1 is a promising approach to abolish tumor-immune resistance. Changes in expression (particularly decreases) might indicate a better response to subsequent immune checkpoint blocking antibodies, suggesting an optimal neoadjuvant treatment setting.

analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: MPM cells and healthy donor peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC), specifically PBMC co-cultured with NCI-H2731 MPM cells. Also referenced in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.
analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Protein Level (Expression assessed by flow cytometry; percentage of positive cells and intensity/MFI values)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Mostly downregulated or unaltered across various chemotherapeutic treatments (cisplatin, oxaliplatin, pemetrexed), with no clear overall trend in general MPM co-cultures. However, a significant alteration (p = 0.037) was noted in the percentage of TIM-3 positive cells on PBMC co-cultured with NCI-H2731 after cisplatin treatment (direction not explicitly stated, but implied altered). A small, statistically non-significant trend towards decreased expression was also described in MPM cell lines. No significant differences were found for expression intensity (MFI) in general. Other studies noted lowered/reduced TIM-3 expression after chemotherapy in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.

analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: MPM cells and healthy donor peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC), also referenced in hepatoma cell lines, dendritic cells (DC), NSCLC cell lines, breast cancer cells, ovarian cancer cells, leukemia cells, NSCLC tissue samples, and MPM tissue samples.
analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Protein Level (Expression assessed by flow cytometry; percentage of positive cells and intensity/MFI values, also immunohistochemistry for tissue samples, cell surface expression for cancer cells)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Mostly downregulated or unaltered across various chemotherapeutic treatments (cisplatin, oxaliplatin, pemetrexed) with no clear overall trend. No significant differences were found in the percentage of PD-L1/2 positive cells or its expression intensity (MFI) compared to untreated groups in co-culture experiments. However, a decrease in PD-L1 expression was observed in two out of three MPM cell lines following pemetrexed treatment. Contextual references show mixed effects: increase (cisplatin in hepatoma/NSCLC/DC, paclitaxel in breast/ovarian, doxorubicin in breast, decitabine in leukemia) or decrease (in NSCLC tumor cells responsive to chemotherapy, implied downregulation in unpretreated MPM tissue samples) depending on the cancer type and specific chemotherapeutic agent.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Ligand for PD-1, involved in immune evasion by tumor cells and regulation of T-cell activity, leading to T-cell dysfunction and an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Part of the defense-line against antitumor immune response. High expression levels are correlated with reduced sensitivity to cisplatin.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Treatment of MPM cell lines (NCI-H2818, NCI-H2795, NCI-H2731) in allogeneic co-cultures with healthy donor PBMCs using various chemotherapeutic agents (cisplatin, oxaliplatin, pemetrexed) for 72 hours. Comparisons to other chemotherapies (cisplatin, paclitaxel, doxorubicin, decitabine) in different cancer types and tissue samples were also made.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Its expression level affects the efficacy of anti-tumor immune responses. Higher expression is suspected to contribute to immune-resistant tumors and reduced sensitivity to cisplatin. Decreased expression might enhance the effect of cisplatin treatment or indicate a better response to subsequent immune checkpoint blocking antibodies, suggesting an optimal neoadjuvant treatment setting.

analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Malignant Pleural Mesothelioma (MPM) cell lines (NCI-H2818, NCI-H2795, NCI-H2731)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Approximately 20% decreased cell survival after 72 h of cisplatin treatment (at IC20 values) compared to untreated controls for all cell lines. NCI-H2818 was significantly more sensitive to cisplatin (p = 0.007 vs NCI-H2731, p = 0.008 vs NCI-H2795) and oxaliplatin (p = 0.030 vs NCI-H2731, p = 0.001 vs NCI-H2795). NCI-H2731 was more sensitive to oxaliplatin compared to NCI-H2795 (p = 0.012). No response to pemetrexed was observed across all cell lines. No significant difference in cell survival between cisplatin and cisplatin + pemetrexed treatment groups.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicates cell viability and proliferation; reflects the cytotoxic efficacy of therapeutic agents.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Chemotherapy treatment with cisplatin, oxaliplatin, and pemetrexed (stand-alone or combination) in MPM cell lines for 72 hours.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Reflects the effectiveness of chemotherapeutic agents in inhibiting cancer cell growth and highlights differential drug susceptibility among MPM cell lines, informing treatment selection.
